paras: The 1905 New York West Side race riots were clashes between white and Black residents of Manhattan's West Side tenement blocks in the Sixties, near Tenth Avenue, in July 1905, during which police were accused of clubbing Black men while sparing white attackers. Police Commissioner McAdoo transferred the precinct captain and appointed a committee to study the causes of the riots. The Black press made police conduct the central issue, and the riots prompted a Black defense league and demands for an investigation.

The riots broke out in districts where, a New York correspondent of the Los Angeles Herald wrote on August 1, Black tenements had "crept in among the white tenements"; he counted three serious riots in as many weeks. Former police chief William S. Devery told the New York Times that Black longshoremen walking home from work had been beaten along Tenth Avenue for a month by hoodlums, with no police to help them.

Accounts of the causes differed: the Herald's correspondent traced the riots to a Black man's insulting remark, another's resentment of jeers from white boys, and a third's refusal to make way for a white woman. Benjamin Palmer Ladson, a Black resident of West 64th Street, wrote that the riot of the Friday before August 1 began when a Black man defended an old white peddler from molesting white boys.

During the riots a Black man named Christopher was shot; his wife said he had no connection with the riots and that the police were "in league with the whites." Devery urged a strict investigation of "the recent clubbing of Negroes." The Rev. Dr. W. H. Brooks later charged that police had clubbed unarmed men in the station house, "causing the death of others," though he named none of the dead. A Mississippi weekly reported that detectives at pawn shops arrested scores of Black people buying or redeeming firearms, and that riots during this roundup left "many wounds and at least one death."

Commissioner McAdoo moved Captain Cooney out of the precinct, a step the Evening Post, quoted by the New York Age, called inadequate. The Post called Cooney "known to be unfriendly to the Negroes," and a Tribune letter writer complained in mid-August that he had been transferred to the Bronx rather than dismissed. McAdoo also received three Black ministers who presented facts about the riots and appointed a committee to study their causes.

In response, the local National Negro Business League, the Colored Republican and Colored Democratic clubs and several pastors, led by Gilchrist Stewart and a minister, held two meetings toward a permanent Afro-American defense league. Preaching at St. Mark's church, Brooks demanded an investigation, the suspension of guilty officers and the arrest of instigators of either race, and denounced the "white washing of the officers." The National Afro-American Council's call to its Detroit meeting listed the riots, "on the part of the police officers, scandalous," beside the lynching of seven men at Watkinsville, Georgia.

In New York the sharpest white criticism came in letters: the New-York Tribune printed Ladson's "Negro Asks Square Deal" and a letter headed "Police Brutality" accusing police of "hounding the negroes and goading them into acts of violence." The Los Angeles Herald's headline said whites "Nearly Murder Blacks," yet its correspondent attributed each riot to a slight by a Black man. The Lexington Advertiser in Mississippi blamed New York's "bad niggers" and wrote that a race row was likely to end in "a thrashing for the police."

The Black press, by contrast, made the police its subject: the New York Age ran "Even Devery Whacks Police" on its front page and covered the defense league and Brooks's sermon at length. The Indianapolis Freeman concluded that the riot was "prompted alone by the cussedness of white toughs" and that the chief of police had distorted the facts, and it reprinted the Council's call.

The Black press, Ladson and Devery placed the provocation on white toughs and hoodlums, while the Herald and the Lexington Advertiser blamed Black men's remarks, refusals or weapons, citing no sources. Deaths are asserted only by Brooks and the Mississippi paper, and neither names the dead or says how many there were.

bases: The Black press and white critics centered on police clubbing, arrests and station-house beatings of Black men during the riots (A2, A5, A9, A12), with attacks by white 'toughs' as the setting (A2, A6).

accounts.label: Black residents and ministers
accounts.gist: White ruffians attacked Black men and the police sided with the whites, clubbing Black men in the street and the station house.

accounts.label: Ex-chief Devery and the Evening Post
accounts.gist: There was no 'Negro riot'; Black longshoremen had been beaten by hoodlums for a month, and the police clubbed Negroes; Cooney's transfer was not enough.

accounts.label: Los Angeles Herald correspondent
accounts.gist: Three riots in three weeks, each set off by a slight between a Black man and whites, in mixed tenement districts.

accounts.label: Mississippi editorial
accounts.gist: A 'bad' armed Black element and white reprobates fought; police took thrashings and rounded up Black men buying guns.

framing.detail: The New York Age ran 'Even Devery Whacks Police', reprinted white critics, and reported the defense league and Brooks's sermon on police brutality.
The Indianapolis Freeman's editorial blamed 'the cussedness of white toughs' and accused the chief of police of distorting the facts.
New-York Tribune letters ('Negro Asks Square Deal', 'Police Brutality') accused the police of siding with whites and hounding Negroes.
The Los Angeles Herald headline said whites 'Nearly Murder Blacks' but attributed each riot to a Black man's remark or refusal.
The Lexington Advertiser blamed New York's 'bad niggers' and dwelt on Black men's revolvers.

versions.value: White toughs, hoodlums or ruffians started the trouble and attacked Black men
Riots began with a Black man's insult, resentment of gibes, or refusal to make way for a white woman
An armed Black 'bad' element and white reprobates both sought fights

conflicts.note: The Black press and New York critics, including a former police chief, place the provocation on whites; the out-of-town white accounts do not name sources for their versions.

versions.value: Police clubbing in the station house caused deaths
At least one death in riots during the firearm roundup (race not stated)

conflicts.note: Neither report names the dead; the other articles mention injuries only.

record_check.dossier: The riots took place in July 1905; August 8 is the date of a separate Harlem fight involving Policeman John Elliott
Elliott was a policeman injured in the separate Aug. 8 Harlem fight; no 'Moody' appears; the named victim of the West Side riots is Christopher, who was shot
police_violence: police clubbing and station-house beatings during white-Black riots
No lynching; deaths are claimed without names
Unnamed deaths claimed by one minister and one Mississippi paper; no count or name
Beatings, police clubbing, a shooting, mass arrests; no property damage or raids on Black-owned businesses reported
Police officers, with white 'toughs' as street attackers

record_check.record: Police raided Black-owned businesses, took owners to the 88th street station; Moody killed; Christopher beaten
record_check.dossier: No raid, 88th Street station or Moody appears; Christopher was shot; police were accused of clubbing Black men, including in the station house

info: July 1905 (several riots in the weeks before August 1; Devery interviewed on July 20; one riot on the Friday before the August 1 letter)
Tenement districts of Manhattan's West Side, the blocks in the Sixties and along Tenth Avenue
Black residents of the West Side; a man named Christopher was shot; Black longshoremen beaten on Tenth Avenue; unnamed men clubbed in the station house
New York police (clubbing, arrests, station-house beatings) and white 'toughs' or 'hoodlums'
Claimed but not counted or named: Brooks said station-house clubbing caused 'the death of others'; a Mississippi paper reported 'at least one death' in riots during the firearm roundup
No report of the dismissal or prosecution of any officer was found; the captain was transferred
